text:
Mycobacterium tuberculosis is an ancient and deadly 
human pathogen that encounters varying environmen-
tal conditions during its complex infection cycle. After 
inhalation, M. tuberculosis infects alveolar macrophages, 
which impose several stresses on the bacterium. It 
replicates in macrophages, which produce cytokines 
and recruit more immune cells to the site of infection 
(Box 1). Initial infection is followed by the formation 
of a granuloma, a dynamic nodule of pulmonary tissue, 
immune cells and bacteria, which can contain the infec-
tion but is also necessary for transmission. M. tubercu-
losis grows rapidly during the initial stages of infection. 
Sometimes the infection directly progresses, resulting 
in necrotic tissue damage, irritation, coughing and 
aerosol transmission. In other cases, the infection stops 
at the granuloma stage, resulting in a non-​contagious, 
static infection that may progress later or never1. 
Infection states are a continuum, and each granuloma 
within a patient is somewhere on the spectrum between 
rapid bacterial growth and dissemination, and complete 
arrest with sterilization by the immune system2–4. As the 
mycobacterial cell envelope is the interface with the host, 
its structure and responsiveness to immune factors are 
important in determining the state of an infection.
The protective cell envelope is composed of the 
cytoplasmic membrane, cell wall, surface lipids and a 
capsule, and is populated by numerous proteins (Fig. 1). 
Biochemical fractionation5 and electron microscopy 
experiments6,7 have characterized the mycobacterial 
cell wall core, which contains peptidoglycan, arabino-
galactan and mycolic acid layers. Its defining feature is a 
waxy outer membrane, the mycomembrane, that is rich 
in mycolic acids8. The outermost structure is a capsule, 
a loose matrix of glucans and secreted proteins that has a 
role in host interactions and virulence9. Numerous pro-
teins are required to build and control the mycobacterial 
envelope (Fig. 1b). These include sensory signalling fac-
tors such as kinases, transporters, regulators of cell wall 
synthesis, cytoplasmic cell wall precursor enzymes and 
periplasmic cell wall assembly proteins.
Considerable evidence indicates that the mycobacte-
rial cell envelope is enormously plastic and highly regu­
lated10–12. But how does regulation actually change the 
structure of the cell wall during human infection? The 
answer to this question is important, because regulation 
of the cell wall affects immune responses13 (Box 1) and 
determines sensitivity to antibiotics14–18 (Box 2). The goal 
of this Review is to interpret information about myco-
bacterial cell envelope organization and regulation in the 
context of an M. tuberculosis infection. Many excellent 
reviews describe the structure8, chemistry19–22 and func-
tion of the mycobacterial cell envelope23–25. Here we will 
focus on the dynamics of this structure.

MreB and deposit new cell wall material asymmetrically 
at the tips of the bacilli26,27. In addition, mycobacteria

The mycobacterial cell envelope  
— a moving target
Charles L. Dulberger1,2, Eric J. Rubin   2,3 and Cara C. Boutte   4*
Abstract | Mycobacterium tuberculosis, the leading cause of death due to infection, has a 
dynamic and immunomodulatory cell envelope. The cell envelope structurally and functionally 
varies across the length of the cell and during the infection process. This variability allows the 
bacterium to manipulate the human immune system, tolerate antibiotic treatment and adapt to 
the variable host environment. Much of what we know about the mycobacterial cell envelope 
has been gleaned from model actinobacterial species, or model conditions such as growth 
in vitro, in macrophages and in the mouse. In this Review , we combine data from different 
experimental systems to build a model of the dynamics of the mycobacterial cell envelope 
across space and time. We describe the regulatory pathways that control metabolism of the cell 
wall and surface lipids in M. tuberculosis during growth and stasis, and speculate about how this 
regulation might affect antibiotic susceptibility and interactions with the immune system.

macro­molecules26,27 (Fig. 1a). It is thought that this spatial 
variability in cell envelope metabolism leads to diverse 
responses to antibiotics and host immunity.
Growth of the mycobacterial cell wall requires 
highly coordinated and localized protein machineries 
anchored in the inner membrane25 or concentrated in 
membrane microdomains near growing cell poles28. 
Enzymes required for elongation and division are local-
ized by polar and septal scaffolding complexes directed 
by DivIVA29–31 and the FtsZ contractile ring, respec-
tively. Many cell wall enzymes28,31 and regulators have 
polar or septal localization during active growth32, which 
results in an envelope with spatially organized metabo-
lism. Studies with fluorescently labelled d-​amino acids 
demonstrated that most new peptidoglycan in myco-
bacteria is deposited at the tips and septal sites33–35. In 
Mycobacterium smegmatis, the penicillin-​binding pro-
teins (PBPs), which catalyse d–d (meso-​diaminopimelic 
acid (mDap)–d-​Ala) crosslinks between peptide stems 
in peptidoglycan synthesis, seem to insert new pepti-
doglycan at the poles and septum. l,d-​Transpeptidases, 
which catalyse l–d (mDap–mDap) crosslinks, are 
localized preferentially along the lateral walls of the cell. 
Thus, peptidoglycan chemistry likely varies across the 
length of the cell, with d–d crosslinks at the poles and 
septum and more l–d crosslinks at the middle of the 
cell36 (Fig. 1a).
Arabinogalactan and mycolic acid synthesis and 
assembly are also localized at the growing poles and 
division septa. Mycolic acid synthesis enzymes, such 
as InhA37, display polar localization, as do the serine/
threonine protein kinases (STPKs) that regulate their 
activity32. The secreted mycolyltransferases that integrate 
mycolic acids into the mycomembrane (the fibronectin-​
binding proteins, also known as antigen 85 (Ag85))38 and 
the arabinogalactan glycosyltransferase GlfT2 (ref.28) 
are also predominately polar and septal. Metabolic 
probes that monitor the activity of mycolyltransferases 
indicate that mycolic acids are integrated mostly at 
septal and polar sites, with greater accumulation at the 
old pole38. Peptidoglycan and mycomembrane biosyn-
thesis are also temporally coordinated at septal sites in 
a sequential process: peptidoglycan is laid down first, 
before the mycomembrane39.
Asymmetric growth is promoted by loss of asym-
metry mutant A (LamA), part of the divisome40. LamA 
localizes to the septum, where it interacts with the PBP 
PonA1 and inhibits growth at the developing new pole. 
LamA generates heterogeneity in cell length and drug 
susceptibility between cells in a genetically identical cul-
ture40. Asymmetric cell division likely also contributes to 
daughter cell heterogeneity. However, the mechanisms 
underlying division site selection are poorly understood 
in mycobacteria and there are conflicting observations 
regarding septal placement41–43. Mechanisms that gener-
ate phenotypic diversity may help M. tuberculosis cope 
with the varying stresses encountered during infection 
and treatment, thus increasing the likelihood that some 
cells will survive.

through co-​evolving with the human immune system, Mycobacterium tuberculosis has generated exquisite mechanisms 
of immunomodulation and immune evasion, many of which depend on its cell envelope. a comparison of cell envelope 
components between M. tuberculosis and ancestral species has revealed a restructuring of the mycomembrane glycolipid 
components, including the mycolic acids and free lipids of the outer leaflet. relatively polar, hydrophilic phenolic 
glycolipids and lipooligosaccharides have been replaced with a more apolar set of phthiocerol dimycocerosates (PDiMs), 
and acyl trehelose glycolipids. these changes likely contribute to the higher hydrophobicity of M. tuberculosis compared 
with ancestors, which may increase transmission through aerosolization116.
M. tuberculosis persists and thrives amidst antibacterial innate and adaptive immune responses. Phagocytes detect, 
engulf and destroy bacteria via phagosomal acidification and other assaults117 while initiating local and systemic 
responses. to launch adaptive immune responses, macrophages and dendritic cells travel to immune hubs such as the 
lymph nodes, where they activate and recruit T cells to granulomas by presenting lipid antigens on their CD1 molecules  
to T cell receptors. CD1 proteins have antigen-​binding grooves that bind and present specific lipid moieties, and  
the CD1 family (CD1a–CD1d) has evolved to present a variety of mycobacterial lipids, including mycolic acids118–120, 
sulfoglycolipids121, lipoarabinomannans122 and phosphatidylinositol mannosides123. recognition of mycobacterial antigens 
by a diverse array of T cells13,118,119,124,125 initiates clearance of infected cells and cytokine responses125,126. the B cell-mediated 
antibody response also has an important role in protection127 and containment of M. tuberculosis infection128.
M. tuberculosis interferes with innate immune signalling pathways, for example, by masking pathogen-​associated 
molecular patterns with PDiM112 and inhibiting toll-​like receptor 2 with sulfoglycolipids129. these strategies inhibit 
detection of bacteria and activation of cytokine responses129 and recruit naive rather than microbicidal macrophages  
to sites of infection112. M. tuberculosis also prevents detection by targeting the antigen presentation pathways of the 
adaptive immune system. M. tuberculosis uses diverse mechanisms for altering the processing and availability of peptide 
antigens for MHC class I (ref.130,131) and MHC class II (ref.132) and CD1-presented glycolipid antigens, which are potent 
stimulators of T cells133,134.
Mycobacterial cell surface components directly compromise killing in the phagosome. secreted proteins of the type vii 
ESX secretion systems and Pro–Glu (PE)–polymorphic GC-​rich repetitive sequences (PGRS) superfamily have been 
implicated in the disruption of membranes135–138 and phagolysosome maturation139–141, which may enable bacteria to 
escape and replicate in the cytosol of infected leukocytes. PDiM, together with the esX-1 system, initiates rupture of 
phagosomes142 and directly protects against reactive nitrogen species143. trehalose dimycolate is also thought to have a 
role in blocking phagosome–lysosome fusion and promoting granuloma formation144,145. trehalose dimycolate protects 
against killing by macrophages in early, active phase infection and promotes necrotic caseation in mature granulomas110, 
which leads to release of bacilli into the airways to be exhaled and transmitted.

Studies of mycobacterial ultrastructure and protein 
localization have mostly been limited to cells in logarith-
mic phase culture, so it is not possible to say how spa-
tial organization and asymmetry may differ under the 
stresses that M. tuberculosis encounters during infection. 
In nutrient-​poor conditions, M. smegmatis differentiates 
into short, less aggregated bacilli with increased long-​
term starvation survival and tolerance to antibiotics15,44. 
These ‘small resting cells’ are more homogeneous in 
morphology44 and show delocalization of some com-
ponents of the cell wall machinery45. Potentially, log-
arithmic phase conditions in M. smegmatis, when cell 
heterogeneity and asymmetry are greatest, most closely 
mimic rapid growth conditions in M. tuberculosis. We 
expect that cell-​to-cell heterogeneity of M. tuberculosis 
under stasis is likely due more to environmental var-
iations within the infection site than to asymmetric 
growth mechanisms.
Temporal regulation
Limitations and assumptions. It is extremely difficult 
to study bacterial physiology during human infection. 
What we know is largely derived from bacteria that are 
found in sputum or from explanted lungs from patients, 
which both represent narrow subpopulations of infec-
tious bacteria. The tools available to understand the cell 
wall and its remodelling in these samples are very lim-
ited. Thus, much of what we surmise below comes from 
in vitro studies and animal models, which cannot repli-
cate the variability in progression of human infection2. 
To make sense of studies using differing approaches, 
we have made three simplifying assumptions. First, 
M. tuberculosis broadly shows two behaviours: rapid 
growth, which is observed in rich medium in vitro 
and early, active phases of infection; and growth stasis, 
which can be induced by in vitro stresses and adaptive 
immunity encountered during chronic mouse infection. 
Second, in the early stages of infection, M. tuberculosis 
grows rapidly but encounters acid, oxidative, hypoxic, 
osmotic and mild detergent stresses. We can learn about 
this stage from in vitro experiments with these stressors 
at concentrations that do not block growth, early stages 
of mouse infection and macrophage infection experi-
ments. Third, a range of infection states exhibit growth 
stasis, including the chronic phase of mouse infec-
tion and stages of subclinical infection in primates and 
humans. M. tuberculosis is thought to replicate, albeit 
slowly, during chronic mouse and subclinical primate 
infection46,47; thus, when we refer to ‘stasis’, we mean that 
growth and death are in equilibrium, not that growth is 
arrested. In stasis, M. tuberculosis is exposed to adaptive 
immunity, very low oxygen levels, detergents, and oxi-
dative and osmotic stresses. We can learn about these 
states from chronic stage mouse experiments48 and 
from in vitro experiments in starvation, late stationary 
phase and oxygen deprivation49, during which growth 
stasis is observed. We expect that many of the stresses 
encountered in these models are also encountered in 
humans. Although these model conditions lack much 
of the heterogeneity in primate infections, they enable 
us to build models for cell envelope regulation from 
available data. We hope these models can be tested 
as new technologies support experiments in more 
complex systems.
Cytoplasmic membrane. The mycobacterial cytoplasmic 
membrane contains standard membrane lipids such as 
the glycerophospholipids, but also has phosphatidy­
linositol mannosides (PIMs), and lipomannans (LMs) 
and lipoarabinomannans (LAMs), which are derivatives 
of PIMs5,50. PIMs likely contribute to the low permeabil-
ity of the mycobacterial cell envelope and intrinsic tol-
erance to antibiotics50. PIMs, LMs and LAMs are critical 
for cell wall integrity51 and for immune manipulation52.
PIMs, which are exclusively found in actinomycetes23, 
are phospho-​myo-inositols attached to one to six man-
nose residues. These are anchored in the membrane with 
one to four fatty acid chains linked to various sites on a 
1-phospho-2-mannose myo-​inositol base (PIM1), mak-
ing AcPIM1. PIMs with four mannose residues (AcPIM4) 
are thought to be transported from the inner leaflet to 
the outer leaflet of the cytoplasmic membrane53, and 
they are the precursors of higher PIMs such as PIM6, 
and the precursors of LMs and LAMs54.
We predict that PIMs predominate in rapid growth 
and are downregulated in stasis (Figs 2,3). This model 
is based partly on data indicating that PIM trans-
port is inhibited by the universal stress protein (USP; 
Rv2623)55. Transcription of usp is downregulated in 
logarithmic phase56 and activated by the response reg-
ulator DosR57. USP is activated by the STPK PknG53. 
DosR and PknG are thought to be more active during 
stasis. Phosphorylated USP binds Rv1747, the putative 
PIM transporter, reducing the number of PIMs on the 
cell surface53. Thus, it seems likely that fewer PIMs are 
present during stasis when USP is upregulated. This 
is corroborated by transposon sequencing data showing 
that pimE, the gene that directs precursors towards 
higher-​level PIM synthesis rather than synthesis of 
LMs and LAMs54, is less important for survival in 
chronic phase mouse infections than in active phase 
mouse infections48. PIMs and LMs strongly induce 
the cytokines that help establish the granuloma58, so the 
high relative levels of PIMs during rapid growth in 
early stages of infection may promote progression of 
the infection.
In our model, LMs and LAMs have the opposite 
expression pattern of PIMs: they seem to be moderately 
expressed in rapid growth and abundant in stasis. LMs 
have long, branched mannose chains attached to PIM4, 
whereas LAMs have additional, branched arabinose 
chains, capped with mannose residues, attached to the 
LM base20. The levels of LMs and LAMs increase sub-
stantially deep in stationary phase, with the LAMs also 
having longer arabinose chains14. Two genes required 
for LM synthesis, lpqW and mtxS, are both upregulated 
during starvation59, whereas other synthesis genes, embC 
and mptA, are downregulated in alveolar macrophages 
during early infection60. This shows a trend for genes 
involved in the synthesis of LMs and LAMs to be upregu­
lated during stasis and downregulated during growth.

arabinotransferase, is upregulated more than embA

These data support the model that LAM levels are high

PIMs, LMs and LAMs, especially the last of these, 
activate Toll-​like receptor 2 signalling58, which in 
M. tuberculosis infection downregulates MHC class II 
antigen presentation and enables infected antigen-​
presenting cells, such as macrophages and dendritic cells, 
to evade killing by T cells62. Thus, high levels of LAMs 
in the chronic phase may help protect static granulomas 
against sterilization by the immune system.
Peptidoglycan. Peptidoglycan maintains cell shape and 
fortifies the plasma membrane against the osmotic 
pressure of the cytoplasm. It is composed of linear 
strands of alternating N-​acetylmuramic acid and 
N-​acetylglucosamine (GlcNAc) sugars crosslinked by 
peptides63 into a layered, honeycomb structure64 (Fig. 4a).
The STPK PknB is the master upstream regulator 
of peptidoglycan metabolism65 during active growth.

PknB detects the status of peptidoglycan metabolism 
through its interaction with the peptidoglycan pre-
cursor lipid II, which localizes and controls the kinase 
activity of PknB66. The first dedicated enzyme in pep-
tidoglycan precursor synthesis, MurA, is indirectly 
activated by PknB. MurA is inactive by default and is 
activated when PknB phosphorylates CwlM, a regula-
tor. Phosphorylated CwlM binds and activates MurA67. 
Unphosphorylated CwlM is membrane associated and 
interacts with the lipid II flippase MviN (also known as 
MurJ)68, possibly regulating it to control flux through 
the precursor synthesis pathway. PknB also phosphory­
lates MviN, which may inhibit flippase activity by 
recruiting the putative MviN inhibitor FhaA69. Thus, 
PknB likely detects periplasmic lipid II and may inhibit 
MviN to prevent too much lipid II from accumulating 
in the periplasm before it can be incorporated into the 
peptidoglycan matrix. PknB also phosphorylates 
the cytoplasmic domain of PonA1, a bifunctional PBP, 
which seems to restrict the rate of cell elongation70. 
In our model, these regulatory events keep peptido­
glycan metabolism chugging along evenly during active 
growth when PknB is expressed59 (Fig. 4b).
Transcriptional downregulation of pknB during sta-
tionary phase71, starvation59 and hypoxia72 implies that 
PknB is not active during stasis. This downregulation 
probably helps broadly downregulate cell wall metabo-
lism72, which decreases the permeability of the wall15 and 
increases antibiotic tolerance17. Decreased expression of 
lytic transglycosylases also implies that peptidoglycan 
turnover decreases in stasis73.
Peptidoglycan is crosslinked by PBP transpeptidases, 
which work within large complexes of regulators and 
other enzymes25. The PBPs PonA1 and PonA2 oper-
ate in largely distinct genetic networks74, which prob-
ably correspond to protein complexes. Transposon 
sequencing data imply that PonA1 is important for 
M. tuberculosis growth during the active phase of mouse 
infection48,70, whereas PonA2 is important during the 
chronic phase48. Therefore, we propose that the PonA1 
complex predominates in peptidoglycan expansion 
during active growth and the PonA2 complex is more 
active in peptidoglycan remodelling during stasis. 
The PonA1 and PonA2 enzyme complexes have dif-
ferent antibiotic sensitivities18,74, implying that these 
complexes are functionally distinct.
The peptidoglycan that is made in logarithmic phase 
and deep stationary phase does not differ by the amount 
or type of crosslinking75, so the chemical structure of 
peptidoglycan may be the same in the active and static 
phases of infection. Peptidoglycan stimulates both innate 
and adaptive immunity through the pattern recognition 
receptor NOD2 (ref.76). Thus, the high levels of peptido-
glycan produced in the active phase may activate innate 
immune cells to clear infections in some cases, but may 
promote the maturation of the granuloma through 
recruitment of lymphocytes in infections that proceed.
Arabinogalactan. The middle layer of the cell wall core 
is made of arabinogalactan sugars. Arabinogalactan 
polymers are connected to peptidoglycan with a 
rhamnose–GlcNAc linker disaccharide, in which the 
GlcNAc attaches to the N-​acetylmuramic acid residues 
in peptidoglycan and the rhamnose binds to galactan 
polymers19 (Fig. 3a). Branched arabinose chains are 
linked to certain galactose residues in the galactan. 
Arabinose sugars are transferred in the periplasm to 
both arabinogalactan and LAM from the lipid-​linked 
precursor decaprenylphosphoryl-​β-d-​arabinofuranose 
(DPA)19 (Fig. 3a).
Because arabinogalactan is covalently attached to 
peptidoglycan, it is likely that its metabolism keeps pace 
with peptidoglycan expansion during active growth. In 
our model, arabinogalactan metabolism decreases in sta-
sis; this is most apparent in the regulation of the galactan 
and linker unit genes, which participate in arabinoga-
lactan — but not LAM — synthesis. Four genes involved 
in galactan and linker unit assembly, rmlB, rmlC, cpsA2 
and glfT2, are transcriptionally downregulated during 
starvation59. PknG inhibits RmlA, a linker unit enzyme, 
by phosphorylation77. PknG is required for M. tubercu-
losis to survive during chronic phase guinea pig infec-
tion78, so this RmlA inhibition likely happens during 
stasis. Thus, it seems that galactan and the linker unit are 
downregulated in stasis. The arabinose polymers in ara-
binogalactan are the same as the ones in LAM, and they 
require complex regulation because arabinogalactan and 
LAM are differentially regulated.
The arabinotransferases EmbA, EmbB and EmbC 
synthesize branched arabinan polymers on arabino-
galactan and LAM, using decaprenylphosphoryl-​β-d-​
arabinofuranose as a precursor19. EmbA and EmbB 
specialize in synthesis of arabinogalactan79 and likely 
predominate in growth, whereas EmbC mostly makes 
LAM80 and seems to be more highly expressed in stasis. 
The embA, embB and embC genes are adjacent to each 
other and can be transcribed together or separately81.

Mycolic acids, trehalose monomycolate and trehalose 
dimycolate. The mycomembrane is composed of lipids, 
glycolipids and secreted proteins. Its outer leaflet is 
composed mostly of mycolic acids, which can be free 
or attached to trehalose sugar to make trehalose mono­
mycolate (TMM) or trehalose dimycolate (TDM)21 
(Fig. 5a). The inner leaflet is made of mycolic acids 
covalently attached to the underlying arabinogalactan 
of the arabinogalactan–peptidoglycan matrix8 (Figs 1,2). 
The myco­membrane contributes to the impermeability 
of the mycobacterial envelope, which is 100–1,000 times 
less permeable to β-​lactam antibiotics than the Gram-​
negative envelope87. Mycolic acids consist of 2-alkyl, 
3-hydroxy long-​chain fatty acids, in which the lipid 
at the 2 position, called the α-​chain, is saturated and 
22–26 carbons long. The lipid on the 3-hydroxyl, 
the mero­mycolate, is 42–62 carbons long (Fig. 5a). The 
α-​chain and the first several carbons of the meromycolate 
are synthesized by fatty acid synthase I (FAS-​I) enzymes. 
FAS-​II enzymes then elongate these chains into the 
meromycolates. Modifications of mycolic acids include 
desaturations and either cis or trans cyclopropana-
tions that bend the meromycolate chain back on itself, 
as well as addition of hydroxy, keto and methoxy groups 
oriented towards the polar edge of the membrane21. 
The modified meromycolates and the α-​chains are 
combined to make mycolic acids before export (Fig. 5a).
As mycolic acids are an essential structural part of the 
cell wall core, their synthesis must keep up with growth 
during early stages of infection (Fig. 5b). The transcrip-
tion of the FAS-​I genes fas, accD4 and accD5 seems to 
correlate with growth59,60,88. The FAS-​II enzymes are all 
inhibited through phosphorylation by PknA, PknB and 
other STPKs89–93. PknA and PknB are expressed during 
growth; their role in regulating FAS-​II enzymes is likely 
to keep mycolic acid synthesis coordinated with peptido-
glycan expansion. PknH, PknD, PknL and PknF can also 
phosphorylate various FAS-​II enzymes. As these STPKs 
are associated with stasis conditions14,72,94,95, we predict 
that their phosphorylation of FAS-​II enzymes reduces 
mycolic acid synthesis during stasis and chronic phases 
of infection.

the first-​line antibiotic treatment for Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection is 6 months long and includes four drugs. 
isoniazid inhibits mycolic acid synthesis, rifampicin inhibits transcription, ethambutol inhibits arabinogalactan synthesis 
and the target of pyrazinamide is uncertain. Developing drug regimens that reliably sterilize infections in less time than 
the current treatment is a major public health goal. One reason antibiotic treatment of M. tuberculosis infection is so 
lengthy is that most drug targets are less active during stasis, so inhibiting them has little effect. Human infections likely 
always include at least some M. tuberculosis cells that are in stasis2. a possible strategy for faster-​acting drug regimens is 
to include drugs that target factors that are active in stasis. in the following paragraphs, we review the work on the 
regulation of key cell wall drug targets.
Penicillins are ineffective against M. tuberculosis, but some work has been done to explore the usefulness of 
carbapenems, which target both penicillin-​binding proteins and l,d-​transpeptidases146. in Mycobacterium smegmatis, 
peptidoglycan construction for growth occurs mostly through penicillin-​binding proteins36, which therefore may be poor 
drug targets during stasis. l,d-​transpeptidases catalyse peptidoglycan remodelling36. Ldta may be upregulated in stasis59, 
and LdtB is required for chronic phase survival147. thus, carbapenems could be effective against M. tuberculosis in stasis.
Ethambutol is a first-​line drug that inhibits the arabinotransferases EmbA, EmbB and EmbC148. inhibition of 
arabinogalactan synthesis by ethambutol inhibits growth, but it is not bacteriocidal149. ethambutol treatment in stasis 
may mostly inhibit lipoarabinomannan (LAM) synthesis by EmbC, which may interfere with the immunomodulatory 
functions of LaM62 and destabilize the cell wall51. therefore, ethambutol may sensitize M. tuberculosis to other drugs and 
to immune clearance. this effectiveness activity profile in growth and stasis may also apply to the benzothiazinethione 
class of drugs that inhibit Dpre1, which helps make the acylated precursor for arabinogalactan and LaM synthesis150,151.
isoniazid inhibits inha, a member of the fatty acid synthase ii pathway that lengthens lipids for mycolic acid synthesis. 
through phosphorylation, PknH92 may substantially downregulate inha activity in stasis14, thus making M. tuberculosis 
less sensitive to isoniazid, as is observed in starvation17. Isoniazid sensitivity is also affected by the catalase–peroxidase 
KatG, which activates the prodrug isoniazid into its active form. KatG expression levels determine isoniazid sensitivity 
in clinical strains152. expression of katG is controlled by the transcription factor Fura, which likely represses its 
expression in stasis153. thus, lower levels of katG in the chronic phase also make isoniazid less effective. However, cell 
wall growth does not completely cease during the chronic phase46,47, so isoniazid does not completely lose its 
effectiveness101.
the mycolic acid synthetic enzyme FadD32 is inhibited by diarylcoumarins, a drug class in preclinical development154. 
FadD32 is highly transcribed in growth60 and likely downregulated in stasis59, so inhibitors of this enzyme are unlikely  
to be effective in stasis. several classes of drugs, some of which are in clinical trials, have been reported to inhibit the

this may be because these drugs dissipate the proton motive force, not because of direct activity against MmpL3 (ref.159),

proximal cis-​cyclopropanes of cis/cis-​meromycolates96,97 
(Fig. 5a). pcaA is transcriptionally upregulated in the 
active phase60, and blocks phagosome–lysosome fusion96 
and stimulation of the pro-​inflammatory cytokine

which implies that cis cyclopropanations are impor-
tant for early stages of infection. PknF inhibits PcaA 
by phosphorylating it96, which may help to enforce 
dormancy in the chronic phase94. mmaA2 and cmaA1, 
which catalyse the distal cis cyclopropanations on cis/cis-​
meromycolates, are downregulated by the stress regula-
tor Rel88 or by starvation59. From these data, we propose 
that cis/cis-​mycolic acids predominate in growth and are 
downregulated in stasis.
We have not found consistent evidence that the 
enzymes that add the methoxy and keto groups to oxy-
genated meromycolates are regulated, but if the cis/cis-​
meromycolates are downregulated in stasis, we expect 
the relative levels of these oxygenated meromycolates to 
increase in stasis. The methoxy mycolic acid synthase 
MmaA4 is more important in the chronic phase than 
the active phase of mouse infections48,98, supporting the 
idea that oxygenated modifications predominate in 
stasis. Oxygenated meromycolates promote toler-

stasis,99 and increase the resistance of M. tuberculo-
sis to several antibiotics during growth18, whereas the 
cis-​cyclopropanes either have no effect or slightly pro-
mote antibiotic sensitivity18. Thus, the relative decrease 
of cis/cis-​meromycolates in stasis likely promotes 
antibiotic tolerance.

Mycolic acids can be esterified to the arabinoga-
lactan and become part of the inner leaflet of the myco­
membrane, remain free or be esterified to trehalose, 
resulting in TMM or TDM, which are in the outer leaflet. 
M. tuberculosis has three mycolyltransferases, FbpA, 
FbpB and FbpC (also known as Ag85A, Ag85B and 
Ag85C), which can all esterify either arabinogalactan or 
trehalose102,103. However, FbpC specializes in mycolyla-
tion of arabinogalactan104, whereas FbpA and FbpB are 
more efficient at making TMM and TDM102,105.
FbpA, FbpB and FbpC are differentially expressed, 
implying that the requirement for TDM does not 
strictly correlate with cell wall growth. In our model, 
TDM levels are relatively high compared with the levels 
of arabinogalactan-​esterified mycolic acids during 
rapid growth. fbpB expression and fbpA expression 
increase during growth65,106, resulting in high TDM 
levels and low levels of free mycolic acids14,65,107,108. MtrA 
and PknA or PknB activate transcription of fbpB and 
fbpA65. Comparisons of fbpA and fbpB mutant strains 
imply that high levels of TDM are more important 
than efficient mycolylation of arabinogalactan during 
early stages of infection104,109. TDM is required to block 
phagosome–lysosome fusion and permit growth in the 
macrophage110, so the high ratio of TDM to mycolated 
arabinogalactan is likely important for progression of 
infection. On entry into stasis, production of TMM and 
TDM decreases107, whereas the levels of free mycolic 
acids increase14 and production of mycolylated arabino-
galactan keeps pace with the slowed growth rate. This 
change is likely partly mediated by the stress regulator 
Rel, which downregulates fbpA and fbpB and upregulates 
fbpC88. Downregulation of PknA and PknB in stasis59 
should also decrease fbpA and fbpB expression65. Stasis 
induces a redistribution of trehalose into the cytoplasm 
as TDM and TMM levels decrease107; this change may 
help permit the establishment of subclinical infection 
as TDM levels on the surface decrease. It also remodels 
carbon metabolism in the cytoplasm in ways that stabi-
lize ATP levels, thus protecting M. tuberculosis against 
antibiotics such as bedaquiline that kill by decreasing 
ATP levels111.
Phthiocerol dimycocerosate. The surface lipid phthio­
cerol dimycocerosate (PDIM) is crucial for infection112. 
This is partly explained by its ability to mask pathogen-​
associated molecular patterns of the cell wall from the 
innate immune system, enabling M. tuberculosis to recruit 
naive rather than microbicidal macrophages112. PDIM 
may also facilitate phagosomal rupture and induction 
of the infection-​promoting type I interferon response113,114. 
The DosR system activates transcription of hrp1, a PDIM 
synthesis factor113, during short-​term and long-​term 
oxygen deprivation57,115. Additionally, several PDIM genes 
are downregulated during starvation59 and hypoxia108. 
Thus, PDIM synthesis seems to be high during active 
growth and downregulated in stasis (Figs 2,3).
Final thoughts
The pathogenesis of M. tuberculosis depends on its hetero­
geneous, dynamic and immunoregulatory cell envelope. 
Mycobacterial pathogens have a number of intricately 
integrated regulatory systems to remodel their cell enve-
lopes, across both space and time, in response to chang-
ing environmental signals (Figs 3,4,5). We may talk of 
‘the’ mycobacterial cell envelope; however, in reality, 
there are numerous, chemically distinct mycobacterial 
cell envelopes that exist in different cells at different infec-
tion stages. The particular cell envelope of a mycobacterial 
cell at any given moment partly determines how that cell 
will respond to the immune system and antibiotics.

asymmetric growth and envelope remodelling to gener-
